title: Should the default JTAG IDCODE be 0x1?
body:
https://github.com/freechipsproject/rocket-chip/blob/9002e7e53299598027f41b95dba1666310923699/src/main/scala/rocketchip/DebugTransport.scala#L22

```scala
class JtagDTMKeyDefault extends JtagDTMConfig(
  idcodeVersion = 0,
  idcodePartNum = 0,
  idcodeManufId = 0,
debugIdleCycles = 5) // Reasonable guess for synchronization.
```

Should the default IDCODE be 0x1, or the same as in the previous debug module (0x10e31913)? Or should it throw an error message to prevent rocket from elaborating if the JTAG is enabled but the idcode is not specified?

@mwachs5 @palmer-dabbelt @ducky64

fix_commits.messageHeadline: Add a note to wire up jtag_mfr_id
Add a note to wire up jtag_mfr_id (#778)

comments.body:
The IDCODE (0x10e31913) uses SiFive's assigned JEDEC Manufacturer ID. So in general those who aren't SiFive should not be using that IDCODE. That's why we removed it from the default.

Those using rocket-chip repo should probably override this default value to something meaningful for their design. The ManufId is actually exported from the ExampleTop as part of its I/O and is tied off in the TestHarness.

I see, that makes sense. Thanks for the explanation. Would having an elaboration-time warning for users of rocket-chip be useful so that they don't run into surprises when they try to program their cores?

When you say "program their cores" do you mean when using OpenOCD to communicate with them? Is there actually a value that you use there that causes a problem? riscv-openocd is very tolerant of the IDCODE, it may print a warning if it's not the expected ID.

I'm not sure what the elaboration time warning would be because the mfr_id could go all the way out the pins of the chip. I added a runtime warning (so if you ran with simulate it could at least detect illegal idcodes, though the chances you detect an unconnected mfr_id are somewhat low):

https://github.com/freechipsproject/rocket-chip/blob/master/src/main/scala/jtag/JtagTap.scala#L175

Note that if you did actually use the defaults here, then your IDCODE *would* be 0x1, because there is a bit in the IDCODE "always 1":
https://github.com/freechipsproject/rocket-chip/blob/master/src/main/scala/rocketchip/DebugTransport.scala#L230

@mwachs5 Ah, I see. I think I see where my confusion was coming from now.

In https://github.com/freechipsproject/rocket-chip/blob/9002e7e53299598027f41b95dba1666310923699/src/main/scala/rocketchip/DebugTransport.scala#L231 it uses two out of the three `Int`s in `JtagDTMConfig` but doesn't actually 
use the third one. I was confused since I thought that all 3 would be determined at elaboration-time by `JtagDTMConfig`. In my design, I think I left io.jtag_mfr_id unconnected and the synthesis tool tied it at some point to zero.

Perhaps if we are not actually going to use `c.idcodeManufId.U`, perhaps it could be a good idea to put in a comment saying "Please wire up io.jtag_mfr_id to set the mfr_id or something"? The TestHarness I think manually goes and re-retrieves it (or maybe just remove `idcodeManufId` from `JtagDTMConfig` to avoid confusion perhaps).

```scala
  idcode.always1    := 1.U
  idcode.version    := c.idcodeVersion.U
  idcode.partNumber := c.idcodePartNum.U
  idcode.mfrId := io.jtag_mfr_id
```

The comment seems like a reasonable request. Keep in mind that RocketChipExampleTop is just an example top level, and other designs could actually wire up mfrId using the value in JtagDTMConfig,  I think we should leave it there but comment it as you suggest.
Thoughts on https://github.com/freechipsproject/rocket-chip/pull/778 ?

title: Rocket comes out of reset with valid icache data
body:
Certain randomization values can lead to rocket's icache immediately asserting a valid response. In default rocket-chip configurations this doesn't have any affect on the processor because a debug interrupt comes before the processor is ready to begin executing. But if you were to use a tethered interface to bring up the system there would be no need for the debug interrupt at the start.

My issue then becomes a question:
Should I setup mtvec or similar mechanism before the processor is reset? 
Can I rely on the first instruction at the reset vector to be fetched correctly?

```
-      val s2_hit = RegEnable(s1_hit, !stall)
+      val s2_hit = RegEnable(s1_hit, Bool(false), !stall)
```

I think @aswaterman would be the best one to answer this question.

title: PTW incorrectly marks the access fault type for out-of-range non-leaf PTEs
body:
<!-- THIS REPOSITORY'S ISSUES ARE RESERVED FOR FEATURE REQUESTS AND BUG REPORTS. -->
<!-- For support questions related to Rocket Chip, please use [Stack Overflow [rocket-chip]](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/rocket-chip). -->

**Type of issue**: bug report

<!-- choose one -->
**Impact**: unknown

<!-- choose one -->
**Development Phase**: proposal

**Other information**
 <!-- include detailed explanation, stacktraces, related issues, suggestions how to fix, links for us to have context, eg. Stack Overflow, gitter, etc -->

**If the current behavior is a bug, please provide the steps to reproduce the problem:**
In S mode, the PTW gets a valid, non-leaf PTE with a PPN exceeding the physical address space.

**What is the current behavior?**
Rocket-chip checks the PPNs (`!invalid_paddr` in PTW.scala:316) before traversing to the next level of page table. It thens returns `ae_final` to the TLB. However, since the page is non-leaf, it does not have the `r` bit set. Therefore, further a read request to TLB is responded with a page-fault exception.

**What is the expected behavior?**
According to the RISC-V manual 5.3.2, in step 4, if the PTE is valid and `pte.r = 0` and `pte.x = 0`, the PTE is a pointer to the next level of page table. Since we have not finished the three levels of page table, we continue to step 2 and `a = pte.ppn X PAGESIZE` to calculate the base address. If accessing the PTE violates the PMA, it should raise an access-fault exception.

This is the same behavior as in Spike. As seen in `mmu_t::walk`, if the PTE points to the next level of page table and does not have any bits of `PTE_D | PTE_A | PTE_U | PTE_N | PTE_PBMT` set, then we calculate the next base address with `base = ppn << PGSHIFT;` and continue to the next iteration of the for loop. In the next level, if accessing the PTE violates PMA (like exceeding the physical address space), an access-fault exception is raised.


**Please tell us about your environment:**
<!--    (examples)
    - version: `git commit hash`
    - OS: `Linux knight 4.4.0-92-generic #115-Ubuntu SMP Thu Aug 10 09:04:33 UTC 2017 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux`
-->
Found during co-simulating rocket-chip with riscv-isa-sim. Page-fault is delegated so rocket-chip goes to S mode while the Spike goes to M mode because of access-fault.
```
   mode different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x0000000000000003, wrong = 0x0000000000000001
mstatus different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x8000000a000060a2, wrong = 0x8000000a000060a8
sstatus different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x8000000200006022, wrong = 0x8000000200006020
   mepc different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x0000000000011186, wrong = 0x000000000001116e
   sepc different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x0000000000010a1a, wrong = 0x0000000000011186
  mtval different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x0000003f9bdf749e, wrong = 0x0000000000000000
  stval different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x0000003f9c07ffac, wrong = 0x0000003f9bdf749e
 mcause different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x0000000000000005, wrong = 0x0000000000000002
 scause different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x000000000000000f, wrong = 0x000000000000000d
```

**What is the use case for changing the behavior?**
Just to align the behavior with Spike and the ISA. I don't think it would be a serious issue for users.

I notice the `pte_addr` is shortened after traversing to the next level. So I think it would be a little bit complicate to fix the behavior by allowing it traverse to the next level. Probably we should just set `ae_ptw` instead in this case.

Please correct me if I'm wrong. If the bug is confirmed, I can submit a PR to fix it.

Probably I'm still missing the condition of reserved bits. Only if the non-leaf PTEs are valid and its PPN refers to an invalid address should we raise access-fault, because accessing the next-level PTE would violate the PMA.

Besides, I found that there may be a separate bug in the page-fault condition in PTW. Currently it checks only the most significant reserved bits (`val pf = pte.v && pte.reserved_for_future =/= 0.U`). However, as discussed in https://github.com/riscv-software-src/riscv-tests/issues/352, non-leaf should not have any of D, A, and U bits set. Therefore, rocket-chip needs to check the D, A, U bits as well for page-fault.

I believe rocket-chip's page-fault condition then would become exactly the same as Spike:
```
if (pte & (PTE_D | PTE_A | PTE_U | PTE_N | PTE_PBMT))
  break;
```

So there would be two separate bugs, for page-fault and access-fault respectively.

The missing cases are:
- access-fault: (1) it is a valid non-leaf PTE; (2) its PPN refers to an invalid address.
- page-fault: a non-leaf PTE has any of D, A, and U bits set.

I've updated two commits to fix the two issues respectively.


Besides, since `resp_ae_final` would have lower priority than page-fault and `ae_ptw` access-fault, we don't need to shrink its condition and keep the condition as simple as possible. 

- page-fault for reserved, non-leaf PTEs: https://github.com/poemonsense/rocket-chip/commit/2a005655d2487fdb0da4e7a526abfff348d2aecb

I had a similar problem. The relevant Solvnet article suggested that I had conflicting versions of VCS installed, which was not a problem in my case.

The issue for me was that gcc by default uses slightly different linker options on Debian/Ubuntu than on Fedora (which is what VCS is tested on). To fix this it I added -LD_FLAGS -Wl,--no-as-needed to the list of vcs options. That means a full command would look something like

vcs -full64 +v2k top.v -LDFLAGS -Wl,--no-as-needed
For more details on this see this SO post.

title: Data access replay error when crossingType=NoCrossing
body:
I'm using a design based on the SiFive Freedom E310, and I'm seeing 2 cycles of latency between the Rocket core issuing a data access and it appearing on the tile's TileLink interface.

The subsystem's config had RocketCrossingParams with crossingType = SynchronousCrossing(). I switched to NoCrossing to see if this would reduce the latency, and if so by how much.

It did indeed reduce the latency by 1 cycle each way.

However I then noticed an issue where the DCache would issue a valid pulse whilst the TileLink address bus ready was deasserted, then issue an s2_nack back to the rocket core, but when it replayed the access the address would be incorrect.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1271666/48977757-b12cf480-f0f4-11e8-96d5-a9b864b7eb30.png)


What happened is an offset calculation has been repeated, corrupting the address. My disassembly looks like so:

```
  1c007e:       10050537                lui     a0,0x10050
  1c0082:       0b050513                addi    a0,a0,176 # 100500b0 <spi_load+0xfe9001e>
  1c0086:       f14025f3                csrr    a1,mhartid
  1c008a:       058a                    slli    a1,a1,0x2
  1c008c:       95aa                    add     a1,a1,a0
  1c008e:       4188                    lw      a0,0(a1)
  1c0090:       8502                    jr      a0
```

The issue is that the ```add a1,a1,a0``` occurs again (the core executes and completes the instruction at 0x1c008c a second time), resulting in an incorrect address in a1.

I've often wondered why the rocket core seems to replay instead of stalling while the various hazards or buses clear. Anyway, does this look like a real bug, and not a configuration issue? Is rocket supposed to work with NoCrossing?

Our design has moved on a little bit since I filed the issue and I haven't been able to recreate the failure.

We are using some custom instruction fetch logic, and I can't rule out the bug being there. I thought I checked it at the time but I didn't store the waveform and I have fixed bugs in the frontend since I filed this. So this is likely a false alarm, sorry about that.

However, I do have an observation about a new issue I now see with the NoCrossing configuration. In trying to recreate this scenario, I configured 4 rocket harts with crossingType=NoCrossing again, and re-run our software. I then noticed the software wasn't progressing and noticed a deadlock of sorts. There is a semaphore register that 3 cores are attempting to claim (atomic swap instruction) and one core trying to release it by writing zero. The system becomes deadlocked because the hart trying to clear the register happens to see a deasserted ready from the tilelink bus every time it attempts the write.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1271666/49697107-7607e680-fc07-11e8-8883-88af7ca90074.png)

I notice when we do have SynchronousCrossing set, the valid out from the tile is held until ready is asserted and the transaction is acked by the bus.

I guess the only way to get this behaviour is with SynchronousCrossing? I presume it'd take changes in the dcache to change the behaviour with NoCrossing?

Thanks again for looking into this. If I do see anything like this in future I'll be sure to save the trace.

**Other information**

In `rocket/DCache.sv`, `pma_checker` is connected as follows (https://github.com/chipsalliance/rocket-chip/blob/master/src/main/scala/rocket/DCache.scala#L269):

```scala
pma_checker.io <> DontCare
pma_checker.io.req.bits.passthrough := true.B
pma_checker.io.req.bits <> s1_req
```

This connection seems to miss out most fields in TLBReq. Crucially, `vaddr` is not connected.

Currently the only usage of pma_checker's response is to set `s2_pma` when TLB is not ready, which is possible in some cases (e.g. if the type of memory operation is prefetch or fence). It seems to me that prefetches are not handled in DCache right now, and IIRC individual fences are not affected by PMAs? So the `pma_checker` code path is mostly redundant? If that's the case, can we remove them all together? If that's not the case, then this may be a bug.

This is found during the effort to convert rocket-chip to chisel3 (#3110), which changed the bi-directional connection semantic to disallowing missing fields in either side of the connection.

comments.body:
> So the `pma_checker` code path is mostly redundant?

To fully understand the `pma_checker` we have to go back to the commit ["Expose DTLB access port"](https://github.com/chipsalliance/rocket-chip/pull/2270/commits/dc68c21e8e5662c81fba003a7579123735c757ef) which introduced this module.

In that commit, a `tlb_port` IO was added to `DCache`, and `DCache` has to handle requests from both `cpu` and `tlb_port`. In cases when we only have requests from one of them, requests are handled through `tlb` and everything is fine.

However, when we have requests from both of them, things become tricky. the author allowed one certain case: when the request from cpu is a physical address and has no exception. In all other cases, request from cpu is nacked.

https://github.com/chipsalliance/rocket-chip/blob/70ed8b63bd3780b2c6091a9e9fbfd12ab9145200/src/main/scala/rocket/DCache.scala#L265 

For that specific case, `pma_checker`, which is an extra TLB, only uses the PMPChecker part (that's why passthrough is always asserted true.B) and handles the request from cpu.

However, the author did not connect the request properly. `s1_req` is not of type `TLBReq` and has no `vaddr` field and should be manually connected in the following way instead of a bulk connection; but, Chisel2 allowed such connection and did not care about the unconnected port.

```chisel
  pma_checker.io.req.bits.vaddr := s1_req.addr
  pma_checker.io.req.bits.size := s1_req.size
  pma_checker.io.req.bits.cmd := s1_req.cmd
  // extra field from later commits
  pma_checker.io.req.bits.prv := s1_req.dprv
  pma_checker.io.req.bits.v := s1_req.dv
```

Fortunately, rocket-chip itself never used the extra `tlb_port` and is not affected. So the title should be changed to "PMA is not working in Rocket Core DCache when there are requests from cpu and tlb_port"

😂 That's not just any rando dependency. 😂  That's a much more (~4x conservatively) performant FIRRTL compiler that produces better, more readable Verilog output. 😉 

Note that on the Chisel side, we are intending to make this download automatically handled like a normal Java dependency. @jackkoenig has an experimental approach that will download this for you from Maven. It's slightly more complicated than normal as it's a binary dependency and not a Java dependency and this has taken some time to sort out.

In order to resolve the dependency issues(and avoid NPM dependency hell as well), In rocket-chip, I choose these solutions:
- for JVM stack-software, use mill for build and dependency management(believe me SBT sucks);
- for dependencies that don't provide a release, use mill to build from source: hardfloat, cde, riscv-opcodes
- for native dependencies, we use nix to manage them, and make it be able to run in different architecture and distros, (e.g. most user use x86, while I'm using an aarch64-linux, some use Ubuntu, while I'm using Arch). for native dependencies, there are two different parts:
1. software for elaboration and emulation, e.g. circt, espresso, verilator.
2. software for test case generation, e.g. riscv-gcc riscv-clang, riscv arch test, riscv tests.

I understand installing nix, and run a daemon for it is not quite straightforward for hardware design users, I aware that, and I'll also try to find some alternative solutions to new users(e.g. provide a docker container and release it)

I hope users understand, we reduces burdens(SBT, legacy Chisel version support, a stable API and a version based backport-flow) since
1. dependencies are hard to manage, there are different ways to manage, see other project from Google, they even depend on a shared cache. Nix may be hard to understand by new users, but it really save our time.
2. build system are hard to manage, mill does have some shortages(e.g. absolute path), but it's almost a state of the art comparing to other different build systems.(SiFive even develop their own build system https://github.com/sifive/wake)
3. We have a limited human resource to manage such a big project. For now only 2 active PhD(I and Jerry) are maintaining it(originally the entire SiFive R&D)

After all, we are still making progress, we may have some breaking change, or even introduce issues that makes some user not happy(like this) in the future, but please understand, our goal  for now is improving the development efficiency to make the rocket-chip continue and alive at least.

As a "downstream consumer" of RocketChip, I (personally) value the
ability to trust the output of a build process by keeping a handle
on all (most?) of the "moving parts". A large part of that is ability
to understand, track, and control the "main" project's dependencies.

It makes sense for a project such as Rocket to depend on a few other
projects that are also "fast-evolving" in their own right (e.g.,
Chisel, mill, etc.).

But in order to maintain any sort of confidence in the output of a
build of the project, as we descend down the tree of dependencies, things
should hopefully settle down into "slow-and-stable", i.e. things that
might be reasonably packaged for a distro (debian/ubuntu/fedora/etc.)
and updated once every few months, if not even less frequently.

many layers deep, then we have an "everything everywhere all at once"
situation that only one or two developers can reasonably keep a handle
on, and anyone else might get lucky to receive a dockerfile of a snapshot
of one of the developers' environments, so as to be able to ritually
"cargo-cult" a rebuild, but without any chance of any control or
understanding of what's going on.

OK, I'm happy to wait for it to stabilize once again. I wish I were
enough of a Chisel/Scala ninja to offer some assistance, but that's
not (yet) the case... :(

title: Issue with DIV result not being written back to register file
body:
<!-- THIS REPOSITORY'S ISSUES ARE RESERVED FOR FEATURE REQUESTS AND BUG REPORTS. -->

<!-- choose all that apply -->
**Type of issue**: bug report

**Other information**
On a Rocket core, I encountered the issue that the although the core accepts the result of the div (div.io_resp_valid & div.io_resp_ready), the data picked for the register file update (rf_wdata) is actually the dmem data. How did the core reach that situation? There is a memory instruction in the writeback state in that cycle that caught a npc_misaligned in the memory stage - so it turns to an exception in WB, allowing the div to write back its result by giving the div.io_resp_ready, but since the npc_misaligned case does not cause the activation of io_dmem_s1_kill, the dcache is free to actually give a response for this memory instruction, in particular, in case of a cache hit, the one that is causing the mux for rf_write to pick the dcache output instead of the div one.
I am attaching a waveform from a Scala-generated RTL. Please ignore the "ILLEGAL" text in the line otherwise showing the instruction - this is a debug signal from out verification environment that currently does not take the full instruction set into account.
Of course, this is on the Rocket level, not a full RocketTile. So can the Frontend deliver a misaligned PC like in this case? In general, it can - I have a configuration where misa is writeable, so take a write to clear the 'c' bit in misa followed by setting bit 1 in tvec followed by an instruction causing an exception. This requests the misaligned PC from tvec at the Frontend which it happily delivers, causing a situation where a non-CFI instruction causes a npc misaligned which is actually a "current PC misaligned".

![npc_misaligned](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/45827187/49926841-d1aeca00-febc-11e8-9922-a0b1ffd194d1.png)

comments.body:
I'm pretty sure something you're doing is violating an implicit property of one of the interfaces.  mem_npc_misaligned should only ever be high for CFIs.

tvec bit 1 is hardwired to 0, so taking an exception can't result in the PC being misaligned.

Well, the attached trace was produced on the RocketTile - it takes some writes to CSRs to disable compressed instructions and then get to the situation where an address ending in ee is requested (value at the cursor position). So it seems in principle, the frontent can deliver misaligned PCs (this was obtained with formal verification - other traces could likely be found as well, this was just the shortest one).
![npc_misaligned_tile](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/45827187/50272330-bb15ef00-0437-11e9-8a17-fc504fa06b4e.png)
I currently do not have a trace where this occurs together with the DIV (getting a cache hit takes more cycles I guess). I just say that in the case that the frontend delivers a misaligned PC, external units like mem are not properly cancelled if requested which may cause issues like the DIV I reported. Form an architecture point of view, it may make sense to have the core also cancel the external requests in mem stage for misaligned - so in the case that is unexpected in the overall system (pc misaligned), the core "just" causes the npc_misaligned, but no other side effects...
Can you please provide the code sequence that corresponds to the waveform?

I am not trying this on software - just on the RTL. But I can extract the sequence of data words provided by the frontend from the simulation trace...
So I see 30199573 followed (CSR update of 301) by 3a082073 (CSR update of 3a0) and 10200073 (CSR update of 102). The next one then is the exception one: 100073 (a break?). The initial register values in the register file were picked as 0. And the initial PC (as it is an input of the RocketTile) was picked as 7ffffff8 (so just 31 bits used, not 38 like in the other issue). The instruction hitting the exception requests 657bcfee as PC.
This is on the RocketTile, so the Frontend is in the model as well.
Can you just send me the waveform? Talking about this over github isn't working.

Thanks for sending the waveform.  I see that stvec[1] is set.  The privileged ISA forbids this; stvec[1] is always supposed to be 0.

It's a situation where the simulation model is more pessimistic than the synthesized result.  The only data source to the stvec register has its bit 1 wired to 0.  (You'll observe this if you try write stvec: stvec[1] will become 0, no matter what you write to it.)  Synthesis will optimize the flop into a constant 0.

That said, there's no reason to have this mismatch.  I'll make a patch to make the RTL simulation better behaved.
I can confirm that the PC no longer gets misaligned, solving the reported DIV issue.
